2   B.   Procedural History

18                            LEGAL STANDARD                               
19        A motion to dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) “tests the legal 
20   sufficiency of a claim.  Rule 8 provides that a complaint must contain a “short and plain statement 
21   of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2).  Thus, a 
22   complaint must plead “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.”  Bell Atl. 
23   Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007).  Plausibility does not mean probability, but it 
24   requires “more than a sheer possibility that a defendant has acted unlawfully.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 
25   556 U.S. 662, 687 (2009).  A complaint must therefore provide a defendant with “fair notice” of 
26   the claims against it and the grounds for relief.  Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555 (quotations and citation 
27   omitted).                                                             
1   true and construes the pleadings in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party.  Manzarek v. 
2   St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 519 F.3d 1025, 1031 (9th Cir. 2008); Erickson v. Pardus, 551 
3   U.S. 89, 93-94 (2007).  However, “the tenet that a court must accept a complaint’s allegations as 
4   true is inapplicable to threadbare recitals of a cause of action’s elements, supported by mere 
5   conclusory statements.”  Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678.                      
6        If a Rule 12(b)(6) motion is granted, the “court should grant leave to amend even if no 
7   request to amend the pleading was made, unless it determines that the pleading could not possibly 
8   be cured by the allegation of other facts.”  Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1127 (9th Cir. 2000) (en 
9   banc) (citations and quotations omitted).  However, a court “may exercise its discretion to deny 
10   leave to amend due to ‘undue delay, bad faith or dilatory motive on part of the movant, repeated 
11   failure to cure deficiencies by amendments previously allowed, undue prejudice to the opposing 
12   party . . . , [and] futility of amendment.’”  Carvalho v. Equifax Info. Servs., LLC, 629 F.3d 876, 
13   892-93 (9th Cir. 2010) (alterations in original) (quoting Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 
14   1962)).                                                               
15                               DISCUSSION                                
16        Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss advances piecemeal challenges to certain claims.  The 
17   Motion does not ultimately seek dismissal of all claims or all Defendants.  Defendants make the 
18   following arguments:                                                  
19     •  (1) Plaintiffs fail to state DTSA and contract claims against Tatarkhanov and Keshtgar 
20        because they do not allege that those individuals took any documents away from Auris; 
21     •  (2) Plaintiffs fail to state valid “information and belief” allegations against Defendants 
22        Romo and Cardona because Plaintiffs acknowledge that they returned trade secret files;  
23     •  (3) Plaintiffs’ injunctive relief claims fail because they only complain of past acts, not 
24        ongoing or future harm, and they seek impermissible and vague “obey the law” 
25        injunctions;                                                     
26     •  (4) Plaintiffs fail to state a claim that their trade secrets were implicated; and  
27     •  (5) the California UTSA preempts the tortious interference and UCL claims. 
1   A.   Failure to State DTSA and Contract Claims against Tatarkhanov and Keshtgar  
2        Defendants argue that Plaintiffs improperly assert DTSA and contract claims against two 
3   new individual Defendants – Tatarkhanov and Keshtgar – without alleging that either of them 
4   actually took any documents away from Auris’s premises.  Plaintiffs counter that they have 
5   pleaded specific facts to adequately state a claim for Tatarkhanov’s and Keshtgar’s 
6   misappropriation of trade secrets and breaches of contract because the allegations are supported by 
7   circumstantial evidence, not merely information and belief.  Further, Plaintiffs contend, even the 
8   information and belief allegations that defendants call conclusory are properly pled under 
9   Twombly, because the allegations (1) are supported by factual information that makes them 
10   plausible, and (2) relate to facts peculiarly in the possession of these two individual defendants 
11   and Noah.  Finally, Plaintiffs argue they have sufficiently pleaded breach of contract claims 
12   against both Tatarkhanov and Keshtgar because both Defendants were contractually required to 
13   return confidential information upon termination of their Auris employment.   
14        A trade-secret plaintiff must show that (1) the plaintiff owned a trade secret, (2) the 
15   defendant misappropriated a trade secret, and (3) the defendant’s misappropriation damaged the 
16   plaintiff.  See 18 U.S.C. § 1836.  “[A] plaintiff who seeks relief for misappropriation of trade 
17   secrets must identify the trade secrets and carry the burden of showing that they exist.”  MAI Sys. 
18   Corp. v. Peak Computer, Inc., 991 F.2d 511, 522 (9th Cir. 1993).  When it comes to proving a 
19   case, the general rule in federal court is that direct and circumstantial evidence are treated alike; 
20   circumstantial evidence is not, by its nature, any weaker than direct evidence. See, e.g., Desert 
21   Palace, Inc. v. Costa, 539 U.S. 90, 100 (2003).  Reliance on circumstantial evidence can be 
22   especially warranted in showing trade secret misappropriation:        

23             misappropriation and misuse can rarely be proved by convincing 
              direct evidence. In most cases plaintiffs must construct a web of 
24             perhaps ambiguous circumstantial evidence from which the trier of 
              fact may draw inferences which convince him that it is more 
25             probable than not that what plaintiffs allege happened did in fact 
              take place. Against this often delicate construction of circumstantial 
26             evidence there frequently must be balanced defendants and   
              defendants’ witnesses who directly deny everything.         
27                                                                         
1   (N.D. Cal. Aug. 24, 2021) (citation omitted); see also UniRAM Tech., Inc. v. Taiwan 
2   Semiconductor Mfg. Co., 617 F. Supp. 2d 938, 944 (N.D. Cal. 2007) (“Circumstantial evidence is 
3   particularly appropriate in trade secret cases.”).                    
4        The Ninth Circuit has clarified that the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard permits 
5   allegations on information and belief where: (1) “the facts are peculiarly within the possession and 
6   control of the defendants”; or (2) “the belief is based on factual information that makes the 
7   inference or culpability plausible.”  Soo Park v. Thompson, 851 F.3d 910, 928 (9th Cir. 2017) 
8   (citing Arista Records LLC v. Doe, 604 F.3d 110, 120 (2d Cir. 2010)).  Nevertheless, “[a] 
9   complaint will not survive a motion to dismiss if it tenders naked assertions devoid of further 
10   factual enhancement.”  Blantz v. Cal. Dep’t of Corr. & Rehab., Div. of Corr. Health Care Servs., 
11   727 F.3d 917, 927 (9th Cir. 2013) (holding that allegations made on information and belief, in the 
12   absence of facts to provide context, were insufficient to avoid dismissal). 
13        Here, Defendants’ attacks the on information and belief allegations against Tatarkhanov 
14   are misleading because they attempt to isolate these allegations from their greater factual context.  
15   Defendants contend that the allegations fall short of establishing that Tatarkhanov misappropriated 
16   trade secrets because his downloads never went outside an Auris-owned device or account, but 
17   Plaintiffs have presented several factual allegations that make the inference of misappropriation 
18   plausible.  In the span of 25 minutes, Tatakhanov downloaded over 60 software quality 
19   management documents from Auris’s Agile System the business day after he resigned.  FAC 
20   ¶ 176.  Tatarkhanov’s download activity that day was unlike any of his prior usage of the Agile 
21   System.  Id. ¶¶ 13, 176.  Within three hours of downloading the information, Tatarkhanov erased 
22   the contents of the hard drive of his Auris computer by reformatting the drive.  Id.  On his last day 
23   at Auris, Tatarkhanov erased the contents of an additional Auris hard drive by reformatting it.  Id.  
24   He reformatted those hard drives without permission, without informing anyone within Auris, and 
25   without a legitimate business purpose.  Id.  When Auris asked Tatarkhanov to explain why he 
26   reformatted his hard drives, Tatarkhanov did not respond.  Id. ¶ 185.  Finally, Tatarkhanov 
27   admitted 18 months after leaving Auris that he had Auris documents in his personal cloud-storage 
1   evidence Plaintiffs do not present on “information and belief,” support those “information and 
2   belief” allegations that Tatarkhanov exfiltrated the trade secret documents and stored them on his 
3   personal storage accounts and computer.                               
4        Defendants’ attack on the information and belief allegations against Keshtgar suffer from 
5   the same flawed approach.  Plaintiffs allege that Keshtgar downloaded dozens of documents 
6   related to design, manufacturing, and testing of Auris’s endoscopes from the Agile System just 
7   days before he left Auris.  FAC ¶ 189.  He had no legitimate business purpose to download those 
8   documents during his last week at Auris.  Id. ¶ 190.  Two years later, Keshtgar admitted that he 
9   “passively retained” Auris documents in his personal email and Google Drive account.  Id. ¶ 192.  
10   Plaintiffs plausibly allege that there was no “passive retention”; rather, Keshtgar actively sent 
11   emails containing Auris proprietary and confidential information to his personal email account.  
12   Id. ¶ 193.  They support this allegation with factual allegations, including that Keshtgar emailed a 
13   photograph that contained undisclosed and trade secret aspects of Auris’s ureteroscope a week 
14   before he resigned.  Id.  That photograph, in combination with the manufacturing process 
15   instructions that Keshtgar had downloaded from the Agile System, described Auris’s setup and 
16   procedure for calibrating and testing a ureteroscope, and that information would be useful to Noah 
17   in developing urology applications.  Id. ¶¶ 193-94.  Finally, Keshtgar also admitted that he had a 
18   confidential Auris spreadsheet in his personal Google Drive account but provided no explanation 
19   how he came to possess it.  Id.                                       
20        The factual allegations recited above show a sequence of events contemporaneous with and 
21   subsequent to Tatarkhanov’s and Keshtgar’s departures from Auris that supports a reasonable 
22   inference that both of them exfiltrated documents from Auris’s Agile System to their personal 
23   accounts and devices to use in their new jobs at Noah.  The inference is particularly reasonable 
24   because Tatarkhanov and Keshtgar transmitted other Auris confidential and/or trade secret 
25   documents outside of Auris: Tatarkhanov to his personal computer and cloud-based storage 
26   accounts, and Keshtgar to his personal email and cloud-based storage accounts.  Id. ¶¶ 179, 192-
27   93.  Such an inference is additionally supported by the suspicious nature of the two Defendants’ 
1   sought to cover up through erasing and/or reformatting hard drives.  Plaintiffs’ allegations may not 
2   encompass every specific aspect of Tatarkhanov’s and Keshtgar’s alleged malfeasance, but the 
3   factual allegations reasonably support an inference that these two Defendants were involved in 
4   specific instances of misappropriation.  See Wisk Aero LLC v. Archer Aviation Inc., No. 3:21-CV-
5   02450-WHO, 2021 WL 8820180, at *15 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 24, 2021) (considering pleading of 
6   misappropriation claims and a defendant’s cherrypicked attack on information and belief 
7   allegations).  Taken together and in sequence, Auris has alleged plausible claims for trade secret 
8   misappropriation against Tatarkhanov and Keshtgar, and the Court therefore denies Defendants’ 
9   motion to dismiss those claims.                                       
10        To the extent Defendants aver that Plaintiffs fail to state claims for breach of contract 
11   against Tatrkhanov and Keshtgar, those contentions fail on similar grounds.  Both defendants were 
12   contractually required to (1) return upon termination of their Auris employment all property 
13   (including confidential information) belonging to Plaintiffs and (2) not retain any confidential 
14   information belonging to Plaintiffs.  FAC ¶¶ 173, 187.  Tatarkhanov admitted that he retained 
15   confidential Auris materials in his personal cloud storage accounts and devices for at least 18 
16   months after he left Auris.  Id. ¶ 179.  Likewise, Keshtgar admitted that he retained confidential 
17   Auris materials in his personal email and cloud storage accounts for at least two years after he left 
18   Auris.  Id. ¶ 192.  Given these admissions, as well as the plausible allegations of misappropriation 
19   discussed above that would violate the contractual terms, Plaintiffs state a plausible claim for 
20   breach of contract.  The Court therefore denies Defendants’ motion to dismiss those claims. 
21   B.   Allegations on “Information and Belief” against Romo and Cardona 
22        Defendants also challenge the sufficiency of the allegations made on “information and 
23   belief” against Romo and Cardona, arguing in substantial part that the allegations fail to state a 
24   claim because, while Romo and Cardona stored or transferred files onto personal devices or 
25   accounts (FAC ¶¶ 88-96, 112-22), Plaintiffs acknowledge that Romo and Cardona “returned” files 
26   to Plaintiffs (¶¶ 106, 124).  Plaintiffs counter that Cardona’s and Romo’s unverified claims that 
27   they returned the subject files are insufficient to moot the DTSA and breach of contract claims 
1        Defendants’ contentions must fail because they avoid full consideration of the FAC, 
2   instead selectively reading portions in isolation.  The FAC makes clear that Cardona and Romo 
3   returned the subject files through their counsel and have not returned the devices to which they 
4   originally downloaded Plaintiffs’ trade secrets.  See FAC ¶¶ 19, 108, 124.  This suggests that, 
5   contrary to Defendants’ manufactured pleading defect, Plaintiffs have not verified that all their 
6   trade secrets were returned by Cardona and Romo.  Even accepting that Cardona and Romo 
7   returned trade secret documents to Auris, Plaintiffs allege that Defendants Cardona, Romo, and 
8   Noah already used the trade secrets to benefit Noah’s business.  FAC ¶¶ 109, 127, 238.  The 
9   alleged use of such trade secrets would not be mitigated or eliminated by the return of the 
10   documents because it is the incorporation of such information into Noah’s operations that creates 
11   Plaintiffs’ alleged ongoing harm.  Further, Defendants cannot establish that returning computer 
12   files means that Cardona and Romo do not continue to have access to some usable form of the 
13   trade secret information.  See East West Bank v. Shanker, Case No. 20-cv-07364-WHO, 2021 WL 
14   3112452, at *13 (N.D. Cal. July 22, 2021) (“To find no likelihood of irreparable harm after a 
15   defendant returns the information it used to misappropriate the trade secrets would render laws 
16   . . . , which seek to protect trade secrets, moot.”).                 
17        Finally, Plaintiffs’ allegations made on information and belief are also supported by 
18   sufficient factual allegations.  The allegations that Defendants Cardona and Romo stored or 
19   transferred files onto personal devices or accounts (FAC ¶¶ 88-96, 112-22) are supported by 
20   sufficient factual context to establish their plausibility at this stage.  In light of the surrounding 
21   context of Cardona’s and Romo’s additional conduct, including their departure from Auris and 
22   hiring by Noah in positions similar to the ones they held at Auris, Plaintiffs plausibly plead 
23   misappropriation and they need not do more at this stage.             
24   C.   Requests for Injunctive Relief                                   
25        Defendants seek dismissal of Plaintiffs’ claims for injunctive relief on multiple fronts, 
26   considered in turn below.                                             
27   //                                                                    
1        1.   Defects in the Prayer for Relief Support Dismissal of Claims 
2        Defendants suggest that the Court should dismiss claims because of shortcomings in the 
3   prayer for relief.  Defendants attack the wrong portion of the pleading.  The appropriateness of the 
4   injunctive relief sought in Plaintiffs’ Prayer for Relief does not resolve the question of whether 
5   Plaintiffs state plausible claims for DTSA and breach of contract pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6), the 
6   subject of the instant motion.                                        

7             The sufficiency of a pleading is tested by the Rule 8(a)(2) statement 
              of the claim for relief and the demand for judgment is not  
8             considered part of the claim for that purpose. . . .  Thus, the selection 
              of an improper remedy in the Rule 8(a)(3) demand for relief will not 
9             be fatal to a party’s pleading if the statement of the claim indicates 
              the pleader may be entitled to relief of some other type.   
10                                                                         
11   Wright & Miller, 5 Federal Practice and Procedure (4th ed.) § 1255, Demand for Judgment – In 
12   General.  In consideration of the instant motion, Plaintiffs’ request for what Defendants consider 
13   an improper injunction does not properly factor in the assessment of the sufficiency of Plaintiffs’ 
14   pleading under Rule 8.  Defendants’ argument against the injunctive relief relies in substantial part 
15   on the insufficiency of the substantive allegations discussed separately.  None of the authority 
16   cited by Defendants stands for the proposition that a claim should be dismissed at the pleading 
17   stage because the injunctive relief sought is somehow improper.  Accordingly, the Court will not 
18   dismiss the claims on this basis.                                     
19        2.   Whether Plaintiffs’ Requested Injunctive Relief is Sufficiently Future-Facing 
20        Defendants argue that Plaintiffs’ claims for injunctive relief against the individual 
21   Defendants fail because they only complain of past acts, not ongoing or future harm.  Plaintiffs 
22   counter that the alleged defects in the prayer for relief do not support dismissal of claims, 
23   especially where Defendants cite no authority for the premise that DTSA claims fail as a matter of 
24   law at the pleading stage because of the purported deficiency of requested injunctions.  
25   Additionally, Plaintiffs aver that the requested injunctive relief is sufficiently future-facing and 
26   tailored to the conduct alleged.  In light of the allegations here, the Court agrees with Plaintiffs. 
27        Courts have considered allegations that an employee downloaded trade secret material to 
1   allegations that the employee had signed agreements with provisions for confidentiality, to support 
2   the former employers’ claim for injunctive relief.  See, e.g., Henry Schein, Inc. v. Cook, 191 F. 
3   Supp. 3d 1072, 1077 (N.D. Cal. 2016); see also Comet Techs. United States of Am. Inc. v. 
4   Beuerman, No. 18-CV-01441-LHK, 2018 WL 1990226, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 15, 2018).   
5        Plaintiffs allege that Defendants engaged in similar conduct.  Plaintiffs aver that 
6   Defendants intentionally took and have not returned all of Plaintiffs’ trade secrets, and that 
7   Defendants have used and continue to use the trade secrets for the benefit of a competitor.  FAC 
8   ¶¶ 106, 108 (Romo); ¶¶ 125-27 (Cardona); ¶¶ 132-41 (Nip); ¶¶ 151-59, 162, 167-69 (Centeno); 
9   ¶¶ 176-85 (Tatarkhanov); ¶¶ 189-99 (Keshtgar); ¶¶ 205-13 (Pandhare); ¶¶ 238-40 (all).  As 
10   discussed above, Defendants’ implication that the taking of trade secrets is mooted by the return of 
11   certain files does not consider the full scope of the allegations against them.  The FAC includes 
12   specific allegations that Defendants did not return all the trade secrets in their possession, posing 
13   an ongoing risk of misappropriation through their use by a competitor.  See, e.g., FAC ¶ 239.  
14   Plaintiffs allege, for example, “On information and belief, Centeno has failed to return all of 
15   Plaintiffs’ files in his possession,” (FAC ¶ 169) and “On information and belief, Centeno and 
16   Noah have used Plaintiffs’ trade secrets in Noah’s business” (FAC ¶ 171).  These allegations are 
17   much more than the failure to “return ‘devices’ in which Plaintiffs allege no ownership interest” 
18   that Defendants glean from Plaintiffs’ pleading, and they do not constitute throwaway contentions.  
19   These allegations about trade secret use are combined with allegations that the individual 
20   Defendants had signed confidentiality agreements that expressly allow either side to petition for 
21   injunctive relief in case of breach.  See, e.g., FAC ¶¶ 144-146 (Centeno’s confidentiality 
22   agreement).  These allegations are sufficient to support injunctive relief of the sort granted in other 
23   DTSA cases.  Defendants’ narrow reading of the operative complaint is too strained, and they are 
24   ultimately incorrect that the injunctive relief sought is insufficiently forward-looking. 
25        3.   Whether Plaintiffs Seek an Improper “Obey the Law” Injunction 
26        Defendants additionally assert that Plaintiffs’ claims fail because courts generally do not 
27   issue so-called “obey the law” injunctions of the type Plaintiffs seek here.  See, e.g., Brady v. 
1   an injunction that essentially requires a party to obey the law in the future is not encouraged and 
2   may be struck from an order for injunctive relief.” (citation omitted)).  Plaintiffs argue that their 
3   requested injunctive relief is sufficiently specific, and Defendants’ argument that Plaintiffs seek an 
4   impermissible “obey the law” injunction is misleading.                
5        Defendants’ attack on so-called “obey the law” injunctions does not follow the law of this 
6   circuit.  “Obey the law” injunctions are not categorically barred in the Ninth Circuit, as 
7   Defendants suggest, and injunctions are instead required to provide sufficient specificity to give 
8   fair notice of enjoined conduct.  SEC v. Murphy, 50 F.4th 832, 852 n.9 (9th Cir. 2022) (the Ninth 
9   Circuit has “not adopted a rule against ‘obey the law’ injunctions per se”).  Even accepting 
10   Defendants’ mischaracterization of Plaintiffs’ prayer for an injunction, and even accepting that 
11   “obey-the-law” injunctions may generally be disfavored, Plaintiffs’ claims need not be dismissed 
12   at the pleading stage on the basis that the relief requested is inappropriate.   
13   D.   Sufficiency of Pleading for Plaintiffs Verb and Cliag
